newsitem.title: FRANCE: Troops in French alert after Paris rush-hour bomb.
newsitem.headline: Troops in French alert after Paris rush-hour bomb.

text.p: France rushed extra police and troops to major cities and border crossings on Wednesday after the bombing of a rush-hour Paris commuter train revived memories of similar attacks in France last year.
"Everything possible will be done to identify and punish those responsible for the attack. We will do all we can to protect our fellow citizens," Prime Minister Alain Juppe said.

He told a hushed National Assembly that the attack bore striking similarities to 1995 attacks by Algerian Moslem rebels. Two people died and 79 others were wounded or in shock after the bombing, including three who remained in critical condition.
Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre said 1,800 soldiers were being assigned to assist police. Most would be assigned to Paris though many would tighten border controls, he said.

The bomb, which exploded on an RER commuter train as it entered the underground Port Royal station during Tuesday's evening rush hour, consisted of a 13 kg (29-lb) gas canister packed with nails, Debre told a cabinet meeting.

Though no one immediately claimed responsibility, the type of bomb as well as the target and timing recalled last year's attacks claimed by fundamentalist extremists fighting Algeria's French-backed military rulers.
Eight people were killed and more than 160 injured in those blasts, which began in July 1995 with a similar train bombing.

"We must be alert to the possibility that this was not an isolated attack," government spokesman Alain Lamassoure said. "The French people must show the same solidarity and sang-froid as they displayed last year," he told Europe 1 radio.

President Jacques Chirac and Juppe praised emergency workers and the French people for their cool in the face of a new terrorist threat. Chirac later convened a meeting of top ministers to confer on the government response to the attack.
Juppe said the investigation was still wide open.
Paris prosecutors said they had asked veteran anti-terrorist magistrates to start a judicial inquiry.
Police chiefs, Interior Minister Debre and Defence Minister Charles Millon called in riot police, gendarmes and troops to put a security operation codenamed Vigipirate back into force.

The plan, put in place during the 1995 bombings but gradually phased out, triggered patrols by police, paramilitary gendarmes and soldiers at public transport stations, public buildings and in the streets.
In a repeat of last year's precautions, commuters were urged to be on the lookout for abandoned packages while school officials were put on alert for suspiciously parked cars.
At the same time, workers began sealing or removing rubbish bins in some public places.

The Foreign Ministry said protective measures were being reinforced at French diplomatic posts. A ministry spokesman said France had also asked its European partners to step up their cooperation in the battle against terrorism.

In financial markets, meanwhile, shares in major French stores groups fell in Wednesday trading on fears that the bomb attack would drive away holiday shoppers in the weeks leading up to Christmas and the New Year, brokers said.
Yves Bonnet, a former head of France's DST counter-espionage service, said: "Only the Algerian Islamic Armed Group (GIA) threatens France with this kind of attack."
After last year's attacks, dozens of suspected Moslem fundamentalists were rounded up and the government said it had destroyed the guerrilla network it blamed for those bombings.
But after Tuesday's blast, officials speculated that other networks might have quickly sprung up in their place.
